summary: Describes a standard method for storing RSA keys and RSA/MD5-based signatures in the DNS, using the KEY and SIG resource record types. It was replaced by RFC 3110.

eli5.summary: This explains how to store one kind of lock-and-signature key in the internet's phone book so others can check a signature.

questions: how do you store rsa keys in dns
subtitle: How to store cryptographic keys and signatures in the DNS.

tldr.problem: The DNS needs a standard way to store RSA public keys and signatures so that DNS responses can be authenticated and the domain system can be used for secure key distribution.
tldr.mechanism: RSA keys are stored as KEY resource records in DNS using algorithm number 1, with the exponent and modulus stored in a defined format. RSA/MD5 signatures are stored as SIG records, computed using MD5 hashing and the RSA algorithm as specified in PKCS #1.
tldr.outcome: DNS can distribute cryptographic keys and authenticate responses, enabling DNS-based security. The RFC was superseded by RFC 3110, which uses DSA and other algorithms.

today: RFC 2537 is a Proposed Standard from March 1999 and was superseded by RFC 3110, which uses DSA and other algorithms for DNS security.

sections.title: DNS Security and Key Storage
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) is the global database that translates domain names like example.com to IP addresses. Traditionally, DNS has no security: you could not verify that a response is actually from the real server or that it has not been tampered with. RFC 2535 extended DNS to include digital signatures and cryptographic keys, turning it into a repository for authentication.

This RFC specifies how to store RSA keys in DNS. RSA is an asymmetric encryption algorithm where a public key is known to everyone and a private key is held secret. The public key can verify signatures made by the corresponding private key, allowing others to confirm that a DNS record or message truly came from the holder of the private key.
sections.eli5: DNS is like a phone book. We want to put your lock (public key) in the phone book so people can check your signature on messages and know it is really from you.

sections.title: RSA KEY Resource Records
sections.content:
RSA public keys are stored in DNS as KEY resource records (RRs) using algorithm number 1. The key data is stored in a specific binary format. The exponent (the public exponent used in RSA operations) comes first, followed by the modulus (a large number that is part of the key). The exponent is variable length, represented by 1 byte if it is 1 to 255 octets long, or by 3 bytes (a zero followed by a 2-byte length) if longer than 255 octets.

The modulus fills the remaining space in the record. Both the exponent and modulus have a limit of 4096 bits to ensure interoperability across implementations. For example, a common approach is a public exponent of 3 or 65537, which minimizes effort to verify signatures. Leading zero octets are not allowed in either field to keep the encoding compact.
sections.eli5: The key is stored as two numbers: the exponent (usually small) and a huge number called the modulus. The format tells you how many bytes the exponent is, then the modulus fills the rest of the space.

sections.title: RSA/MD5 Signatures in DNS
sections.content:
When DNS records are signed using RSA and MD5, the signature is computed in a specific way. First, the data to be signed (determined by RFC 2535) is hashed using the MD5 algorithm, producing a 128-bit digest. Then, the signature is computed by encrypting a structure containing the MD5 digest, along with a fixed prefix that identifies MD5, using the signer's RSA private key.

The computation follows PKCS #1 standard: the encrypted value contains the bytes 00, 01, padding of FF bytes, a 00 byte, an ASN.1 algorithm identifier prefix for MD5 (a fixed sequence of hex bytes), and finally the MD5 hash. The padding is chosen so the total length equals the modulus. Leading zeros are allowed in the final signature, and the signature is transmitted as a binary value in the SIG record.
sections.eli5: To sign something, you hash it with MD5, wrap it in a standard format, and encrypt it with your private key. Others can decrypt it with your public key to verify you signed it.

sections.title: Performance and Key Size Considerations
sections.content:
Signature generation and verification speed differ between RSA and DSA (another algorithm). RSA signature verification is fast when the public exponent is small, such as 3 or 65537. DSA signature generation can be faster with precomputation, but DSA verification is much slower than RSA verification when RSA uses a small exponent, which is recommended for DNS keys.

DNS implementations traditionally optimize for small responses, typically under 512 bytes. Larger key sizes increase record size. It is advisable to minimize the size of KEY resource record sets in the DNS while maintaining adequate security. Each secure zone returns at least one authenticating SIG record along with the KEY records, further increasing response size.
sections.eli5: Small RSA exponents make verification very fast, but bigger keys take more space in DNS responses. It is a balance between security and keeping DNS messages small.
